chapters.title: Patient particulars
chapters.blurb: Maternal age and reproductive history set the background risk before examination

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Note maternal age and parity immediately: maternal age over 35 years substantially raises the risk of chromosomal aneuploidy, while previous pregnancy history identifies recurrent loss and guides subsequent investigations.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness
chapters.blurb: Bleeding character, tissue passage, and cramping pain separate the clinical stages

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Enquire about the exact duration and severity of bleeding and lower abdominal cramping; bleeding soaking more than one pad an hour or passage of grey-white fleshy tissue signals active progression towards inevitable or incomplete miscarriage.

skill.hx.obg.booking_lmp.expect: Calculate the precise gestational age from a reliable last menstrual period and cycle regularity to compare clinical uterine size with expected dates, and verify earlier pregnancy test or scan records.

skill.hx.miscarriag.symptoms.expect: Distinguish mild bleeding without pain in threatened miscarriage from heavy bleeding with rhythmical suprapubic cramps and tissue expulsion in incomplete loss, and ask about shoulder pain or faintness to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Underlying medical conditions, endocrine disorders, and previous pregnancy outcomes

skill.hx.obg.medical_family_drug.expect: Screen for systemic medical conditions including overt hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and exposure to teratogenic drugs or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents.

skill.hx.obg.previous_pregnancies.expect: Record each prior pregnancy in order: consecutive early losses define recurrent pregnancy loss, while a history of mid-trimester painless cervical dilatation points toward cervical insufficiency.

skill.hx.miscarriag.risk.expect: Identify risk factors predisposing to pregnancy loss including advanced maternal age, prior miscarriages, uterine structural anomalies or fibroids, and acquired autoimmune thrombophilias.

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: Haemodynamic stability, pallor, and signs of sepsis

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Assess for acute distress, anxiety, pallor of the conjunctiva and palmar creases, and delayed capillary refill indicating significant blood loss and impending hypovolaemic shock.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Measure pulse and blood pressure carefully: tachycardia and postural hypotension confirm substantial blood loss, while fever, rigors, and tachypnoea point toward septic miscarriage.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Peripheral oedema is absent in uncomplicated early pregnancy loss; its presence alongside hypertension suggests pre-existing chronic renal or vascular disease rather than pregnancy-induced changes.

chapters.title: Pelvic and abdominal examination
chapters.blurb: Speculum inspection of the cervical os and bimanual assessment of uterine size

skill.exam.obg.vulval_inspect.expect: Inspect the vulva and perineum for active blood loss, clots, or conceptus tissue fragments visible at the vaginal introitus.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_inspect.expect: Visualise the external cervical os: observe whether blood or tissue is protruding through the canal, and inspect the ectocervix to exclude local polyps, severe erosion, or trauma.

skill.exam.obg.bimanual.expect: Assess internal os patency (open in inevitable and incomplete, closed in threatened and complete), uterine size relative to dates (smaller in incomplete, matching in threatened), and ensure fornices are free to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

skill.approach.obg.pelvic_close.expect: Clean the patient, ensure she is comfortably repositioned, and immediately provide sensitive, clear communication about the examination findings.

skill.miscarriage.basics.title: Spontaneous abortion and miscarriage: definitions and mechanisms
skill.miscarriage.basics.oneLine: Definition of pregnancy loss before viability, epidemiological scope, and underlying mechanisms
skill.miscarriage.basics.why: Understanding the clinical definition of miscarriage and its biological causes prevents confusing non-viable early pregnancy with bleeding from viable gestation, guides sensitive communication with parents, and establishes the medical basis for expectant, medical, or surgical care.

teach.heading: Definition and gestational limits
teach.body:
Spontaneous abortion, commonly termed miscarriage, is the spontaneous loss of an intrauterine pregnancy before fetal viability.

In international and national guidelines, this threshold is defined as pregnancy loss before twenty to twenty-four completed weeks of gestation, or an expelled fetus weighing less than five hundred grams when gestational age is uncertain.

teach.heading: Epidemiology and timing
teach.body:
Miscarriage is the commonest early pregnancy complication, occurring in ten to twenty percent of clinically recognised pregnancies.

More than eighty percent of spontaneous pregnancy losses take place in the first twelve weeks of gestation. Early losses often manifest as heavy menstruation, whereas later losses involve distinct stages of cervical dilatation and fetal expulsion.

teach.heading: Genetic and developmental aetiology
teach.body:
The single most common cause of early sporadic miscarriage is embryonic chromosomal abnormality, accounting for approximately half of all first trimester losses.

Autosomal trisomies, monosomy X, and triploidy represent the majority of these karyotypic defects. Most chromosomal anomalies arise de novo from non-disjunction during gametogenesis and carry a low risk of recurrence.

probes.q: What is the standard clinical definition of miscarriage by gestational age and fetal weight?
probes.a: Spontaneous loss of an intrauterine pregnancy before twenty to twenty-four weeks of gestation, or the expulsion of a fetus weighing less than five hundred grams.

probes.q: What proportion of early spontaneous miscarriages are attributed to embryonic chromosomal abnormalities?
probes.a: Approximately fifty percent of early sporadic miscarriages are caused by embryonic chromosomal abnormalities such as autosomal trisomies.

skill.miscarriage.findings.title: Clinical stages of miscarriage: physical and pelvic findings
skill.miscarriage.findings.oneLine: Differentiating threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed, and septic miscarriage
skill.miscarriage.findings.why: The management of early pregnancy loss hinges entirely on clinical staging. Distinguishing whether the internal cervical os is open or closed, whether tissue has been partially expelled, and whether intrauterine infection has supervened determines whether observation, medication, or emergency surgical evacuation is required.

teach.heading: Threatened versus inevitable miscarriage
teach.body:
In threatened miscarriage, vaginal bleeding is typically mild, abdominal pain is slight or absent, and the internal cervical os remains closed. The pregnancy remains potentially viable, and ultrasound shows a live intrauterine fetus.

In inevitable miscarriage, bleeding is heavier, rhythmical painful contractions occur, and the internal cervical os is open, with or without membrane rupture. Continuation of the pregnancy is impossible.

teach.heading: Incomplete versus complete miscarriage
teach.body:
Incomplete miscarriage features persistent heavy vaginal bleeding, painful uterine cramps, and a patulous internal os through which conceptus fragments protrude. The uterus feels smaller than the calculated gestational age.

In complete miscarriage, all products of conception have been expelled. Uterine cramps cease, bleeding becomes minimal, the cervical os closes, and the uterus returns to near normal non-pregnant size.

teach.heading: Missed and septic miscarriage
teach.body:
Missed miscarriage describes retention of a non-viable embryo or an anembryonic sac within the uterus. Bleeding is minimal or absent, the os is closed, and earlier pregnancy symptoms regress.

Septic miscarriage occurs when retained products become infected. Features include maternal fever, chills, tachycardia, purulent offensive vaginal discharge, marked suprapubic tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness.

probes.q: What is the critical physical examination difference between threatened and inevitable miscarriage?
probes.a: The internal cervical os is closed in threatened miscarriage, whereas the internal cervical os is dilated and open in inevitable miscarriage.

probes.q: What examination findings distinguish incomplete miscarriage from complete miscarriage?
probes.a: In incomplete miscarriage the cervical os is open with visible tissue and active bleeding, whereas in complete miscarriage the os is closed, bleeding has subsided, and all products have been expelled.

probes.q: What clinical constellation confirms the diagnosis of septic miscarriage?
probes.a: Fever, tachycardia, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, and cervical motion excitation in the presence of early pregnancy bleeding.

skill.miscarriage.summary.title: Synthesising the miscarriage clinical summary
skill.miscarriage.summary.oneLine: Constructing a succinct, diagnostic clinical summary of early pregnancy loss
skill.miscarriage.summary.why: A structured clinical summary allows rapid triage, communicates maternal haemodynamic stability, clarifies the exact stage of pregnancy loss, and outlines the urgent therapeutic priorities to the obstetric team.

teach.heading: Components of the clinical summary
teach.body:
A complete clinical summary must encapsulate maternal age, parity, verified gestational age, nature of vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain, haemodynamic status, cervical os patency, and sonographic confirmation.

Stating these facts in a single coherent statement prevents miscommunication, clarifies the clinical stage, and informs the decision between outpatient medical therapy and inpatient surgical evacuation.

teach.heading: Example summary structure
teach.body:
Consider a typical presentation: A twenty-four year old primigravida at nine weeks gestation presents with six hours of heavy vaginal bleeding, tissue passage, and cramping lower abdominal pain.

She is haemodynamically stable. Examination confirms an open internal cervical os with retained products of conception and a smaller than dates uterus, consistent with an incomplete miscarriage requiring evacuation and anti-D prophylaxis.

probes.q: What core elements must be included in a clinical summary of suspected miscarriage?
probes.a: Gestational age, maternal haemodynamic stability, volume of bleeding, state of the cervical os, and whether products of conception have been expelled.

skill.miscarriage.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of first trimester bleeding and pelvic pain
skill.miscarriage.differential.oneLine: Distinguishing miscarriage from ectopic pregnancy, molar disease, and local cervical causes
skill.miscarriage.differential.why: Early pregnancy bleeding is not synonymous with miscarriage. Ectopic pregnancy represents the leading cause of first trimester maternal mortality, and confusing an ectopic gestation with an incomplete miscarriage can delay life-saving laparoscopy. Hydatidiform mole and benign cervical lesions must also be systematically excluded.

teach.heading: Ectopic pregnancy as the critical differential
teach.body:
Ectopic pregnancy presents with amenorrhoea, unilateral pelvic pain, and dark vaginal spotting or bleeding. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy causes haemodynamic collapse, peritoneal signs, and cervical motion tenderness.

Ultrasonography showing an empty uterine cavity with an adnexal mass or free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, combined with serum beta-hCG above the discriminatory zone, confirms ectopic pregnancy rather than miscarriage.

teach.heading: Gestational trophoblastic disease
teach.body:
Hydatidiform mole presents with vaginal bleeding, excessive uterine enlargement greater than expected for gestational dates, severe hyperemesis, and early-onset pre-eclampsia.

Ultrasonography demonstrates a characteristic snowstorm or vesicular pattern without an embryo, accompanied by markedly elevated serum beta-hCG levels often exceeding one hundred thousand units.

teach.heading: Local genital tract and physiological causes
teach.body:
Benign cervical lesions, including endocervical polyps, severe cervical ectropion, and cervicitis, cause postcoital or contact spotting without uterine contractions, with a closed internal os and a normal intrauterine pregnancy.

Physiological implantation bleeding occurs around the time of the missed menstrual period, presenting as transient light spotting without pain, and resolves spontaneously without intervention.

probes.q: What key findings on transvaginal ultrasound distinguish ectopic pregnancy from an intrauterine miscarriage?
probes.a: An empty endometrial cavity in the presence of an adnexal mass or free pelvic fluid on transvaginal ultrasound points toward ectopic pregnancy.

probes.q: What ultrasound feature and clinical finding characterise a hydatidiform mole?
probes.a: A classic snowstorm or vesicular ultrasound appearance and a uterus enlarged beyond calculated gestational dates with markedly elevated beta-hCG levels.

skill.ix.miscarriage.workup.title: Diagnostic workup: transvaginal ultrasound, beta-hCG and laboratory tests
skill.ix.miscarriage.workup.oneLine: Ultrasonic criteria for pregnancy failure, beta-hCG interpretation, and blood tests
skill.ix.miscarriage.workup.why: Transvaginal ultrasound is the diagnostic gold standard for early pregnancy loss, but premature diagnosis risks terminating a viable intrauterine pregnancy. Applying verified measurement thresholds alongside serial quantitative beta-hCG and maternal blood grouping ensures diagnostic accuracy and timely anti-D prophylaxis.

teach.heading: Transvaginal ultrasonography definitive criteria
teach.body:
Transvaginal ultrasound is far more sensitive than transabdominal scanning in early gestation.

Pregnancy failure is definitively diagnosed if the crown-rump length is seven millimetres or greater with no fetal cardiac activity, or if the mean gestational sac diameter is twenty-five millimetres or greater with no visible embryo.

teach.heading: Inconclusive findings and rescan intervals
teach.body:
When ultrasound findings fall below definitive cut-offs, such as an empty gestational sac under twenty-five millimetres or a fetal pole under seven millimetres without heartbeat, the scan is inconclusive.

A repeat transvaginal ultrasound in seven to fourteen days is mandatory before declaring pregnancy failure, preventing inadvertent termination of a healthy earlier pregnancy.

teach.heading: Serum beta-hCG and blood testing
teach.body:
Serum beta-hCG doubles approximately every forty-eight hours in viable early intrauterine gestations. An inappropriate rise, plateau, or fall indicates a non-viable pregnancy or an ectopic gestation.

Maternal blood grouping and Rhesus typing are mandatory for all women with early pregnancy bleeding. A complete blood count assesses the degree of anaemia, while crossmatching is indicated if haemorrhage is heavy.

probes.q: What crown-rump length threshold on transvaginal ultrasound definitively indicates embryonic demise if no heartbeat is seen?
probes.a: A crown-rump length of seven millimetres or greater with no detectable fetal heartbeat definitively confirms embryonic demise.

probes.q: What mean sac diameter threshold without an embryo confirms early pregnancy failure on transvaginal scan?
probes.a: A mean sac diameter of twenty-five millimetres or greater with no visible embryo on transvaginal ultrasound.

probes.q: What should be done if transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty sac measuring eighteen millimetres?
probes.a: Because the mean sac diameter is under twenty-five millimetres, the scan is inconclusive and a repeat scan in seven to fourteen days is required.

skill.miscarriage.diagnosis.title: Diagnostic formulation and clinical staging of early pregnancy loss
skill.miscarriage.diagnosis.oneLine: Formulating the stage of miscarriage, maternal stability, and risk stratification
skill.miscarriage.diagnosis.why: A diagnostic formulation in early pregnancy bleeding must integrate gestational age, physical examination of the cervical os, ultrasound findings, and haemodynamic status. This categorisation directly dictates whether expectant observation, medication, or urgent surgical evacuation is safe.

teach.heading: Synthesising stage and clinical signs
teach.body:
The definitive diagnosis integrates three pillars: the status of the internal cervical os, the presence or expulsion of products of conception, and transvaginal ultrasound evidence.

Threatened miscarriage presents with a closed os and documented fetal viability. Inevitable miscarriage presents with an open os and active bleeding. Incomplete miscarriage presents with an open os and retained conceptus echoes on ultrasound.

teach.heading: Assessing stability and complication risk
teach.body:
Every diagnosed patient must be stratified by haemodynamic stability. Tachycardia, postural hypotension, and pallor indicate substantial blood loss requiring immediate volume resuscitation.

Maternal pyrexia, pelvic peritonism, and foul discharge define septic miscarriage, transforming a routine clinical problem into a life-threatening surgical emergency requiring urgent inpatient admission.

probes.q: What three elements confirm the diagnosis of an incomplete miscarriage?
probes.a: Vaginal bleeding with an open internal cervical os and ultrasound showing retained products of conception in the uterine cavity.

probes.q: When is a patient with early pregnancy bleeding classified as a high-risk emergency?
probes.a: When there is haemodynamic instability from severe haemorrhage, suspected ectopic pregnancy, or features of septic miscarriage such as high fever and pelvic peritonitis.

skill.tx.miscarriage.title: Management of miscarriage: expectant, medical, surgical, and anti-D care
skill.tx.miscarriage.oneLine: Evidence-based management pathways, evacuation methods, anti-D prophylaxis, and supportive counselling
skill.tx.miscarriage.why: Women experiencing miscarriage require individualised care tailored to clinical stage, haemodynamic stability, infection risk, and personal preference. Providing clear choices between expectant, medical, and surgical management while ensuring anti-D prophylaxis and bereavement support promotes physical recovery and psychological healing.
skill.tx.miscarriage.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of drug class and principle. Specific agents, doses, routes and regimens must be taken from your current national or institutional guideline at the time of prescribing. CliniX does not prescribe.

teach.heading: Expectant and medical management
teach.body:
Expectant management involves watchful waiting for seven to fourteen days in stable women with incomplete or missed miscarriage, allowing spontaneous tissue passage. It is successful in over seventy percent of incomplete miscarriages.

Medical management uses vaginal prostaglandin treatment, with or without antiprogestogen pretreatment chosen according to the miscarriage subtype in the current national guideline, to accelerate expulsion of retained tissue, supported by adequate analgesia.

teach.heading: Surgical uterine evacuation
teach.body:
Surgical management by manual vacuum aspiration or electric suction evacuation is indicated for heavy bleeding, haemodynamic instability, infected tissue, or failed medical management.

Manual vacuum aspiration under local paracervical block is safe, portable, and avoids general anaesthesia. Care must be taken to avoid aggressive sharp curettage, which risks uterine perforation and intrauterine adhesions.

teach.heading: Rhesus isoimmunisation prophylaxis
teach.body:
Non-sensitised Rhesus-negative women require anti-D immunoglobulin within seventy-two hours of a sensitising loss: miscarriage after twelve weeks, or earlier loss with excess bleeding, abdominal pain or uterine instrumentation.

In Indian practice, fifty micrograms is given below twenty weeks of gestation and three hundred micrograms from twenty weeks. In British guidance, two hundred and fifty international units is given below twenty weeks and five hundred units from twenty weeks.

teach.heading: Septic miscarriage and bereavement care
teach.body:
Septic miscarriage demands urgent intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and prompt surgical evacuation of infected retained tissue once antibiotic cover is established.

Compassionate bereavement support is an essential component of care. Reassure the woman that early miscarriage is rarely caused by daily physical activities, offer counselling, and discuss future pregnancy planning when she feels ready.

probes.q: What are the indications for immediate surgical evacuation rather than expectant or medical management in miscarriage?
probes.a: Heavy uncontrolled vaginal bleeding, maternal haemodynamic instability, suspected intrauterine infection or septic miscarriage, and patient choice.

probes.q: What is the recommended timeframe and indication for anti-D immunoglobulin in early pregnancy loss?
probes.a: Within seventy-two hours of a sensitising loss in a non-sensitised Rhesus-negative woman, namely miscarriage after twelve weeks or earlier loss with excess bleeding, pain or instrumentation, to prevent maternal isoimmunisation.

probes.q: Why is gentle suction evacuation or manual vacuum aspiration preferred over vigorous sharp curettage?
probes.a: Because suction evacuation significantly reduces the risks of uterine perforation, cervical trauma, and subsequent intrauterine adhesions causing Asherman syndrome.

skill.annex.miscarriage.tvs_criteria.title: Ultrasonographic diagnostic criteria for early pregnancy loss
skill.annex.miscarriage.tvs_criteria.oneLine: Standardised measurement thresholds and rescan intervals for diagnosing early pregnancy failure
skill.annex.miscarriage.tvs_criteria.why: Clear sonographic criteria prevent diagnostic error and ensure that early viable gestations are never inadvertently classified as failed pregnancies.

teach.heading: Standard ultrasound thresholds for miscarriage
teach.body:
Diagnostic thresholds on transvaginal ultrasonography are established by consensus guidelines from international obstetric societies to achieve one hundred percent specificity for non-viability.

Applying these strict criteria prevents false positive diagnoses of miscarriage in early developing intrauterine pregnancies.

probes.q: What is the recommended management when transvaginal ultrasound shows an embryo of five millimetres without cardiac activity?
probes.a: Because the crown-rump length is under seven millimetres, the scan is inconclusive and a repeat scan in seven to fourteen days is required.

cases.title: Early pregnancy bleeding and lower abdominal cramping in a 24-year-old woman
cases.opening: Doctor, I am about two months pregnant and this morning I started bleeding heavily from below with bad cramps in my lower belly.
cases.fallback: I came to the hospital because the bleeding got heavier and I was afraid I might lose my baby.

patient.name: Sunita
patient.occupation: Homemaker, primary caregiver in the household
patient.residence: Peri-urban settlement in Pune district, Maharashtra, lives with husband and parents-in-law

cues: what brings you to the hospital today
what is your main problem today
tell me what happened today
why have you come to the casualty
presenting.reply: Doctor, I missed my period two months ago and confirmed I was pregnant, but since early this morning I have had fresh bleeding down below and severe cramping pain in my lower stomach.

cues: when did the bleeding start
how long have you been bleeding
did the bleeding start suddenly
how many hours ago did it begin
bleeding_onset_duration.reply: The bleeding started about six hours ago when I woke up, at first like light spotting, but over the last two hours it has become much heavier.

cues: how much blood are you losing
how many pads have you soaked
are the pads completely soaked
is the bleeding very heavy
bleeding_amount_pads.reply: In the last two hours I have soaked two thick cloth pads completely, and fresh blood was dripping when I went to use the toilet.

cues: have you passed any blood clots
did you see any fleshy pieces
did any solid tissue come out
have you noticed grey or pink tissue
clots_and_tissue_passage.reply: Yes, about an hour ago I passed two dark red jelly-like clots and then a small, fleshy greyish-white lump came out into the pad.

cues: describe the stomach pain
what does the pain feel like
is the pain like menstrual cramps
does the pain come and go
cramping_pain_character.reply: It is a severe cramping pain right in the middle of my lower belly below the navel. It comes in tight waves every few minutes, just like severe period cramps.

unilateral_pain_shoulder.reply: No, the pain is right across the middle of my lower belly. I do not have sharp pain on one side and my shoulders feel completely fine.

what was the date of your last period
how many weeks pregnant are you
are your periods regular
gestational_age_lmp.reply: My last normal period started exactly nine weeks ago on the twentieth of August. My periods are always regular every twenty-eight to thirty days, and my urine test was positive four weeks ago.

cues: is this your first pregnancy
have you been pregnant before
have you had any miscarriages before
do you have any children
prior_pregnancies_history.reply: This is my second pregnancy. Last year I had an early miscarriage at about seven weeks that cleaned out on its own. I do not have any living children yet.

cues: did you have morning sickness
have your pregnancy symptoms changed
did your nausea suddenly stop
how have your breasts been feeling
pregnancy_symptoms_change.reply: I had terrible nausea and breast soreness for the past three weeks, but over the last two days the nausea suddenly disappeared and my breasts stopped feeling swollen.

cues: have you felt dizzy or lightheaded
did you feel faint when standing up
have you lost consciousness
have you had any blackouts
dizziness_and_fainting.reply: I felt a bit weak and dizzy when getting out of the auto-rickshaw at the hospital gate, but I have not fainted or blacked out.

cues: have you had any fever or chills
did you notice any bad smelling discharge
have you had shivering
has there been any foul smell
fever_chills_discharge.reply: No fever and no chills at all. The blood does not have any foul or bad smell.

cues: do you have diabetes or thyroid problems
do you have high blood pressure
have you been diagnosed with any medical condition
do you have any heart or kidney disease
medical_illnesses.reply: No, I do not have diabetes, high blood pressure, or thyroid trouble, and the doctor at my local clinic said my booking blood tests were normal.

cues: what medicines are you taking
are you taking folic acid
have you taken any painkillers like brufen
did you take any pills to stop or start bleeding
medications_and_folic_acid.reply: I was taking daily folic acid tablets from the local health centre. I have not taken any painkillers, home remedies, or any tablets to cause an abortion.

cues: what is your blood group
do you know your rh factor
are you rh negative
have you ever received an anti d injection
rhesus_and_blood_group.reply: My blood group is B negative, and my husband is B positive. After my miscarriage last year they gave me an injection in my hip, which the doctor called anti-D.

cues: did you have any fall or injury
have you had recent sexual intercourse
did you lift any heavy weights
was there any accident to your belly
trauma_and_intercourse.reply: No, I did not fall down, lift anything heavy, or have an accident. My husband and I have not had intercourse recently.

cues: were you using any contraception
have you ever had an intrauterine copper t
did you use an iud before this pregnancy
were you taking birth control pills
contraception_and_iud.reply: No, we were actively trying for this pregnancy, so I have never used an intrauterine device or birth control pills.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Patient is conscious, oriented, anxious, in mild discomfort from uterine cramps; mild conjunctival pallor present; no peripheral cyanosis, clubbing, or oedema.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 96 beats per minute, regular, good volume; blood pressure 110/70 mmHg sitting; respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute; temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius; oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air.

skill.gen.edema.finding: No pedal or pretibial oedema; face and hands are not puffy.

skill.exam.obg.vulval_inspect.finding: Vulva and perineum show active dark red bleeding; small blood clots and a tiny fragment of fleshy decidual tissue are visible at the introitus.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_inspect.finding: Cusco speculum reveals fresh dark red blood issuing through the external cervical os; the internal os is open and admits a small piece of conceptus tissue; cervix appears otherwise healthy with no polyp or erosion.

skill.exam.obg.bimanual.finding: Bimanual pelvic examination confirms the internal cervical os is patulous and admits one fingertip; uterus is anteverted, soft, enlarged to about six to eight weeks size, smaller than the nine-week dates; fornices are completely free with no adnexal mass or tenderness; no cervical motion excitation tenderness.

tvs.label: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasonography
tvs.result: Endometrial cavity contains irregular, heterogeneous echoes measuring 18 mm with disruption of gestational sac; no viable embryo or fetal heart activity seen; internal cervical os is open; both ovaries and adnexa appear normal with no ectopic gestational sac; no free fluid in pouch of Douglas.
tvs.note: Confirms incomplete miscarriage with retained products of conception and rules out ectopic pregnancy.

blood_group_rh.label: Blood group and Rhesus typing
blood_group_rh.result: B Rhesus negative; antibody screening negative.
blood_group_rh.note: Critical finding: patient is Rh-negative and non-sensitised, requiring anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours.

cbc.label: Complete blood count
cbc.result: Haemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, total leucocyte count 8,200/uL, platelets 240,000/uL.
cbc.note: Mild anaemia secondary to acute blood loss; normal white cell count makes active pelvic sepsis unlikely.

serum_beta_hcg.label: Quantitative serum beta-hCG
serum_beta_hcg.note: Single value below the level expected at 9 weeks gestation, consistent with non-viable early pregnancy; a falling or plateauing trend can only be judged on serial measurements.

urine_routine.label: Urinalysis
urine_routine.result: Normal, protein nil, sugar nil, pus cells 1-2 per high power field.
urine_routine.note: Excludes active urinary tract infection as a contributor to lower abdominal pain.

differentialModel.answer: Incomplete miscarriage at nine weeks gestation. Consider inevitable miscarriage, threatened miscarriage, complete miscarriage, missed miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, gestational trophoblastic disease, and cervical polyp.

diagnosis.answer: Incomplete miscarriage at nine weeks gestation in a B Rhesus-negative woman, presenting with active bleeding and cervical dilatation.

managementModel.answer: Provide immediate analgesia, offer definitive uterine evacuation with manual vacuum aspiration or medical misoprostol therapy, administer anti-D immunoglobulin within seventy-two hours for Rhesus-negative status, and ensure compassionate bereavement counselling.

teachingPoints: The state of the internal cervical os is the central physical discriminator: an open os with active bleeding and tissue passage confirms incomplete miscarriage, whereas a closed os defines threatened or complete loss.
Uterine size smaller than calculated gestational dates reflects partial expulsion of products of conception, which ultrasound corroborates by identifying retained heterogeneous cavity echoes.
Bilateral free fornices with an absence of adnexal masses or cervical motion tenderness are essential physical signs that exclude tubal ectopic pregnancy.

Maternal Rhesus status must never be omitted in early pregnancy bleeding: non-sensitised Rh-negative women with a sensitising loss, namely miscarriage after twelve weeks or earlier loss with heavy bleeding, pain or instrumentation, require anti-D immunoglobulin within seventy-two hours to prevent isoimmunisation.

Manual vacuum aspiration under paracervical local block offers an effective, quiet, portable alternative to electric suction or theatre general anaesthesia in primary and secondary healthcare centres.
Vigorous sharp curettage must be avoided during evacuation of incomplete miscarriage to prevent uterine wall perforation and late intrauterine synechiae.

Bereavement counselling is an integral component of clinical management: reassuring the patient that early miscarriage is predominantly genetic and not her fault alleviates guilt and promotes recovery.
